frameworks.name: Distributor-Layer Revenue Architecture
frameworks.definition: Shifting from direct customer acquisition to acquiring agencies/producers as distribution layers, where each distributor generates multiple recurring customers per year rather than selling episodic customers one at a time.

frameworks.name: Agency Stacking Model
frameworks.definition: Acquiring one new distributor (agency or producer) per month, each generating one customer per month, creating a compounding monthly customer base that stacks year-over-year as prior distributors remain active.

claims.text: For episodic service businesses selling to 20-25 customers yearly with 80% churn, reshaping the business model to acquire agencies or producers as distributors—rather than acquiring end customers directly—creates a stackable, compounding revenue model (Alex Hormozi, moremozi Experiential Marketing segment). Mechanism: each distributor generates multiple customers annually, and once onboarded, becomes a repeating revenue source rather than a one-time sale, transforming the unit of acquisition from 'customer' to 'distributor.'
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: episodic or one-time service delivery model
distributed customer base where producers/agencies hold the relationship
multiple customers per distributor possible annually
claims.mechanism: Each month acquired distributor generates repeating monthly customer volume; distributor churn becomes the binding constraint instead of customer churn; retention at the distributor level compounds whereas customer-level acquisition requires constant replacement.

numbers.axis: Customer acquisition cadence via distributor model

anchors.value: 12 retained distributors → 12 customers/month baseline, plus new 1 distributor added → 13 total customers/month

bounded_by: Assumes 80%+ distributor retention; if distributor churn mirrors customer churn (80%), compounding does not materialize
Requires activated distributor journey with clear incentive alignment
Does not apply to direct consumer sales where end-customer is the ultimate buyer

claims.text: Episodic service businesses (e.g., experiential marketing firms) are constrained by the need to replace 80% of customer base yearly, whereas distributor-acquisition models allow month-to-month stacking where each prior distributor continues generating revenue, creating a compounding business even when the underlying work product is one-time.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service delivery is episodic or project-based
Producers/agencies (not end customers) are the entity controlling demand
Distributor retention can exceed customer retention
claims.mechanism: Customer-level churn forces constant re-acquisition; distributor-level stacking allows prior distributors' ongoing customer generation to compound; distributor becomes the true customer.

numbers.axis: Effective customer retention by acquisition model

anchors.value: Effective retention if 80% of distributors remain active and each generates monthly customers

bounded_by: Assumes clear boundary between distributor/agency and end customer
Does not work if end customer and producer are the same entity

claims.text: When a service business measures success as customer acquisition count (e.g., 20-25 customers per year) without understanding conversion funnel metrics (lead volume, conversations-to-close rate, cost per conversation), the business is 'posting and praying'—making decisions without data visibility into which channels or messages drive results (Alex Hormozi, experiential marketing segment).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Multiple acquisition channels in use (paid search, social media)
No funnel metrics tracked or visible
Monthly budget deployed without ROI feedback

numbers.axis: Spend vs. Visibility in Multi-Channel Campaign

anchors.value: $13,000/month paid search + social spend, no metrics tracked

bounded_by: Assumes channels are measurable; applies less to brand/awareness spend where intent signals are delayed
Does not address situations where metrics infra itself is missing

claims.text: For service businesses with distributed customer relationships (e.g., agency producers located across multiple states), the true primary customer is the producer or account owner who initiates the job request, not the agency itself, even if the agency is contractually upstream.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Producers or account managers hold decision authority on work
Many producers are non-full-time or freelance
bounded_by: Applies to on-demand / episodic service delivery
Does not apply when agency holds P&L responsibility and producers are internal employees

claims.text: Adopting a distributor-layer business model requires designing an activation and incentive journey (e.g., affiliate program, co-marketing support, revenue share) to sustain distributor engagement and retention, mirroring the structure of customer retention programs but operating at the distributor level.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Need to maintain 80%+ distributor retention for compounding to work
bounded_by: Does not specify the exact structure of activation journey
Assumes distributor churn is measurable and optimizable

claims.text: In a distributor-stacking model targeting one new distributor per month, the growth ceiling is determined not by customer acquisition capacity but by the cumulative number of active distributors and their per-distributor customer generation rate; scaling requires keeping prior distributors generating customers while adding new distributors (Alex Hormozi).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Distributor-stacking model is the chosen strategy
Goal is predictable monthly customer volume
claims.mechanism: Each new distributor onboarded increases total monthly customer baseline; prior distributors' continued activity creates a floor that rises monthly, compounding.

anchors.value: 12 distributors (assuming 100% retention) × 1 customer/month = 12 monthly run rate
24 distributors × 1 customer/month = 24 monthly run rate (if 100% retention)

bounded_by: Assumes each distributor generates exactly 1 customer/month; actual variation may be significant
Requires distributor retention to exceed 80%; if distributor churn is high, stacking fails
Does not account for distributor graduation (some may become too large/independent)

examples.text: An experiential marketing firm ($13M top-line revenue, 20-25 customers/year, 80% churn) currently acquires customers by 'waiting for the phone to ring' while spending $13,000/month on paid search and social media without tracking metrics (lead source, conversations-to-close, cost-per-customer). Under a distributor model, instead of acquiring these 20-25 episodic customers, the firm would identify 12 agency producers or agency partners who each source one customer per month to the firm; after 12 months, these 12 producer relationships generate a baseline of 12 monthly customers from just prior-year distributors, allowing growth to compound as new producers are added monthly.

An agency producer located in a different state receives a request to produce a campaign for Coca-Cola; the producer calls the experiential firm to handle production. The producer (not the agency) is the true customer initiating the relationship, because the producer controls when work flows to the firm. If the firm targets the producer instead of the agency, they can establish a repeat relationship where the producer becomes a recurring source of jobs over time, rather than viewing each agency as a one-time contact point.

practices.text: Measure and track paid media performance: establish funnel metrics (lead volume, cost per lead, conversations-to-close rate, cost per customer) for all active acquisition channels (paid search, social, etc.) to eliminate decision-making without data visibility.

Design a producer/agency activation journey that clarifies how distributors make money when they refer customers to your service, including co-marketing support, affiliate commissions, or revenue-share structures.

Shift targeting from agencies to individual producers or account owners; develop outreach strategy that reaches producers at agencies and positions your service as a tool that allows them to win more jobs and increase take-home per job.
